::: {.callout-important title="z is never observed in real time"}
The target $z$ compares the season's **eventual peak** with the largest value seen **so far**. The eventual peak is unknown until the season is over, so a forecaster standing in week $t$ never sees $z_t$: predicting it is the whole forecasting problem. Every value of $z$ in this document was computed **in hindsight**, from completed historical seasons. The document has two jobs: (1) describe the distribution of this retrospective outcome, which a model must learn to predict, and (2) look for **real-time predictors**, quantities that can be computed from data through week $t$ (and, for "historical" quantities, from strictly earlier seasons only) that are associated with the eventual $z$.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Names of models and feature sets"}
Feature sets and model versions are named as in the section *Versions and names used in this document* of the methods document (`peak-models-methods.html`).

- **core**: the 13 default features of `peak_gbqr`.
- **SB**: core plus the 4 synchrony and 2 burden features, available in idmodels as `sync_burden_features = True`.
- **SB + *group***: SB plus a candidate group tested only in this document's cross-validation harness.

In this document the synchrony features use the **reported-at-t** definition: a location must have a report for week $t$. The model runs used the **carried-forward** definition (@sec-predictors).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="How to regenerate" collapse="true"}
The figures, tables and quoted numbers are computed by the R chunks in this document. Python is used only for what needs the model code: building the training rows and features with `idmodels`, and the LightGBM cross-validation. From the repository root:

```bash
VENV=/Users/nick/Documents/research-versioned/idmodels/.venv
export DYLD_FALLBACK_LIBRARY_PATH=$VENV/lib/python3.12/site-packages/sklearn/.dylibs
# 1. export the replay rows (about 15 s)
$VENV/bin/python analysis/peak-models/relative_size_eda.py
# 2. features, leakage checks and cross-validation (about 15 min from scratch; about 1 min reusing cached CV;
#    add --workers 1 to keep the machine light)
OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 $VENV/bin/python analysis/peak-models/relative_size_predictors.py --reuse_cv --reuse_holiday_cv --reuse_lit_cv --reuse_regional_cv --reuse_types_cv
# 3. render (R; about 1 min, less when the knitr cache is warm)
/Applications/quarto/bin/quarto render analysis/peak-models/relative-size-eda.qmd
```

Step 1 writes `eda/replay_rows.parquet` (one row per series and season week, with the model's features and the targets) and `eda/season_arrays.parquet` (the weekly series and running maxima). Step 2 writes `eda/predictor_rows.parquet` (all candidate features), per-row cross-validation scores (`eda/cv_*.parquet`), season-bootstrap comparisons (`eda/cv_bootstrap.csv`), gain importances, the holiday tables and the random-walk check; drop the `--reuse_*` flags to recompute the cross-validation. Shared R helpers are in `R/eda_helpers.R` and `R/relative_size_helpers.R`. Data: ILINet (weighted ILI × percent positive) and FluSurv-NET, final data, from `ilinet-validation/data-ilinet-flusurvnet.parquet`. A companion document, `peak-timing-size-eda.qmd`, describes peak timing and size themselves.
:::

```{r setup}
#| cache: false
source("R/relative_size_helpers.R")
kable <- function(x, ...) knitr::kable(relabel_df(x), ...)  # feature-set names as in the methods document
rows <- read_rows("eda/replay_rows.parquet")
arr <- read_parquet("eda/season_arrays.parquet")
```

# Why a "relative" size target?

## The forecasting problem in one paragraph

Every winter, influenza activity in a US state rises from a low baseline, reaches a highest week (the **peak**), and falls back. The FluSight challenge asks forecasters, week by week during the season, for the **peak size** (the largest weekly value between early October and late May) and the **peak week** (when it happens). We index weeks within a season by **season week**: week 1 is the first week of August, week 10 is roughly the first week of October and week 43 is late May. Weeks 10–43 are the **window** over which the peak is defined. "Week t" below always means "we are standing at season week t and have seen data through week t, but nothing later".

## The running maximum $M_t$

Standing at week $t$, the one thing we know for sure about the peak is that it is **at least as large as the largest value we have already seen in the window**. Call that number the running maximum:

$$M_t = \text{largest in-window value observed in weeks } 10, \dots, t.$$

In words: look back over the season so far (from week 10 onward), and take the biggest week. $M_t$ can only go up or stay flat as the season goes on; it goes up each week that sets a new record, and once the true peak has happened it never changes again. Before the window opens (weeks 5–9 in the training data), there is no in-window history yet, so the code sets $M_t$ to the most recent value. **$M_t$ is known in real time.**

## The target z

The peak models do not predict the peak size directly. They predict how much *bigger* the eventual peak will be than what we have already seen, on a log scale:

$$z_t = \log(\text{eventual peak} + \varepsilon) - \log(M_t + \varepsilon).$$

Plain-language reading: $e^{z_t}$ is the factor by which the season's record still has to grow. $z_t = 0$ means "the peak has already happened; the record will not be broken again". $z_t = 1$ means the peak will be about $e \approx 2.7$ times the current record; $z_t = 3$ means about 20 times; $z_t = 5$ means about 150 times. The small constant $\varepsilon$ ("eps") only keeps us from taking the log of zero. It is 0.01 for FluSurv-NET (hospitalizations per 100,000 people) and 0.001 for ILINet (percentage points of ILI × fraction positive), roughly 1/1000 of a typical national peak in each source (`idmodels.peak.series.LOG_EPS`). A forecast of $z$ is turned back into a forecast of the peak by $\text{peak} = (M_t + \varepsilon)e^{z} - \varepsilon$.

**$z_t$ is not known in real time**, because the eventual peak is not. @fig-realtime shows the difference between what a forecaster sees at week 18 and what we can compute once the season is over.

```{r fig-realtime}
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "**Real time vs hindsight** (Massachusetts, ILINet 2017/18). Left: at week 18 a forecaster knows the series so far and its running maximum $M_{18}$; everything to the right of the dotted line, including the peak, is unknown. Right: after the season we know the peak (star) and can compute $z_{18}$, the log-distance from $M_{18}$ up to the peak. All training data for the models, and every $z$ plotted in this document, are of the right-hand kind."
t0 <- 18
eps0 <- LOG_EPS[["ilinet"]]
a <- arr |> filter(source == "ilinet", location == "25", season == "2017/18", season_week >= REPLAY_START,
                   season_week <= WINDOW[2])
pk_w <- rows |> filter(source == "ilinet", location == "25", season == "2017/18") |> pull(peak_week) |> first()
pk <- a$y[a$season_week == pk_w]
m18 <- a$M[a$season_week == t0]
base <- function(show_future) {
  p <- ggplot(a |> filter(season_week <= t0), aes(season_week)) +
    pre_window(log_y = TRUE) +
    geom_line(aes(y = y + eps0), color = INK2) + geom_point(aes(y = y + eps0), color = INK2, size = 0.9) +
    geom_step(aes(y = M + eps0), color = ACCENT, linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = t0, linetype = "dotted", color = INK2) +
    annotate("text", x = t0 - 0.5, y = (m18 + eps0) * 1.5, label = "M[18]~(known)", parse = TRUE, color = ACCENT,
             hjust = 1, size = 3.2) +
    annotate("text", x = t0 + 0.5, y = 1.4e-3, label = "today: week 18", hjust = 0, size = 3, color = INK2) +
    scale_y_log10("ILI × % positive + eps (log)", limits = c(eps0 * 0.8, pk * 4), labels = plain_log_labels) +
    scale_x_season_week()
  if (!show_future) {
    p + annotate("text", x = 31, y = 0.3, label = "future weeks,\npeak and z:\nunknown", fontface = "italic",
                 color = INK2, size = 3.5) +
      labs(title = "In real time: what a forecaster knows at week t")
  } else {
    p + geom_line(data = a |> filter(season_week >= t0), aes(y = y + eps0), color = "#b7b6b0") +
      geom_point(data = a |> filter(season_week > t0), aes(y = y + eps0), color = "#b7b6b0", size = 0.9) +
      geom_hline(yintercept = pk + eps0, linetype = "dashed", color = BLUE) +
      annotate("point", x = pk_w, y = pk + eps0, shape = 8, color = BLUE, size = 3) +
      annotate("text", x = pk_w + 0.6, y = (pk + eps0) * 1.5, label = paste("actual peak, week", pk_w), hjust = 0, size = 3) +
      annotate("segment", x = t0, xend = t0, y = m18 + eps0, yend = pk + eps0, color = BLUE,
               arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.15, "cm"))) +
      annotate("text", x = t0 - 0.5, y = sqrt((m18 + eps0) * (pk + eps0)),
               label = paste0("z[18] == ", f2(log(pk + eps0) - log(m18 + eps0), 1)), parse = TRUE, color = BLUE,
               hjust = 1, size = 3.2) +
      labs(title = "In hindsight: the rest of the season, the peak, and z", y = NULL)
  }
}
base(FALSE) | base(TRUE)
```

Three reasons for predicting $z$ rather than the peak itself:

1. **It is scale-free, so sources can be pooled.** The models are ultimately used for NHSN hospital admissions, which have only a few usable seasons. ILINet (outpatient visits for influenza-like illness) and FluSurv-NET (lab-confirmed hospitalization rates in a sample of counties) measure the same epidemics in completely different units, but add 10–20 more seasons. A ratio "eventual peak / current record" means the same thing in every source.
2. **It conditions on the stage of the epidemic.** "How much more growth is left?" has a very different answer in November than in February, and for a state still at baseline versus one visibly past its peak. The model's features describing the season so far (`rel_max`, `wks_since_max`, `g1`, …, defined in @sec-stage) are also measured relative to $M_t$ and are all computable in real time, so the model learns a mapping from "where are we on the curve" to "how much is left".
3. **It respects a hard constraint.** The peak cannot be below $M_t$, so $z_t \ge 0$ always. A predictive distribution for $z$ on $[0, \infty)$ builds this in automatically.

The price is that $z$ has an awkward distribution: a lump of probability ("atom") exactly at 0 once the peak has passed, a long right tail early in the season, and a strong dependence on $\varepsilon$ when $M_t$ is tiny. Sections 2–8 look at each of these; sections 9–13 search for better real-time predictors.

## What a training row is

The models learn from **season replay**: for every completed historical season of every location and source, and every week $t$ from 5 to 43 with an observation, we pretend we are standing at week $t$, compute the features from weeks $1, \dots, t$ only, and attach the eventual $z_t$ computed from the completed season. One series (for example "ILINet, Massachusetts, 2017/18") contributes up to 39 rows. Because we use **final** (fully revised) data, once the peak week has passed the eventual $z_t$ is *exactly* 0.

```{r coverage}
n_series <- rows |> distinct(source, agg_level, location, season) |> nrow()
cov_tab <- rows |> group_by(source = group) |>
  summarise(seasons = paste(min(season), max(season), sep = "–"), `n seasons` = n_distinct(season),
            locations = n_distinct(location), series = n_distinct(paste(location, season)), rows = n())
```

**Data used here.** **NHSN is deliberately excluded for now:** its seasons are the held-out test data for the peak models, and looking at them here would contaminate that validation; they may be added back later. We also **drop the ILINet series for Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands** (all seasons) before building rows: their ILINet × percent-positive values are zero all season, so the "peak" is 0, $z$ is trivially 0 and a few pre-window rows had $z < 0$. @tbl-coverage shows what remains: `r format(n_series, big.mark = ",")` series and `r format(nrow(rows), big.mark = ",")` rows. (The companion peak timing/size document counts slightly fewer ILINet state series because it applies the 25-observed-weeks rule before, rather than after, the models' filling of short gaps.)

```{r tbl-coverage}
#| tbl-cap: "Training data used in this analysis. \"series\" is a (location, season) pair; \"rows\" is one per observed season week 5–43. FluSurv-NET has 13 sites plus a national series; ILINet regions are the 10 HHS regions."
kable(cov_tab, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

# The eventual z in individual seasons

```{r fig-ma}
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| fig-cap: "**Massachusetts, three ILINet seasons.** Top: the weekly series (grey), its running maximum $M_t$ (orange staircase) and the eventual peak (star and dashed line), on a log scale so that $z_t$ is the vertical distance between the staircase and the dashed line (the arrow shows it at week 18). Bottom: the eventual $z_t$ by week, computed after the season. Shaded weeks 5–9 are before the window opens."
ili_lab <- "ILI × % pos."
example_row(arr, rows, list(
  list(src = "ilinet", loc = "25", season = "2017/18", title = "Massachusetts, ILINet 2017/18", ylab = ili_lab),
  list(src = "ilinet", loc = "25", season = "2019/20", title = "Massachusetts, ILINet 2019/20", ylab = ili_lab),
  list(src = "ilinet", loc = "25", season = "2012/13", title = "Massachusetts, ILINet 2012/13", ylab = ili_lab)))
```

In all three Massachusetts seasons, $z_t$ comes down in **steps**: it stays flat during weeks in which no new record is set (e.g. 2019/20, weeks 11–16, when activity was at baseline and wobbling below its week-11 value) and drops each week the record is broken. It hits 0 in the peak week and stays there. Early in the season $z$ is 5–8, because $M_t$ is a baseline-level number. The 2012/13 season was early (peak in week 22) and $z$ collapses from about 3 to 0 within six weeks. The staircases also show why "weeks since the max was set" and "how far below the max is the current value" might carry information: just before the peak the series sets a new record every week, while after the peak it falls away from $M_t$.

```{r fig-small}
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| fig-cap: "**Montana**, a small state, same layout."
example_row(arr, rows, list(
  list(src = "ilinet", loc = "30", season = "2017/18", title = "Montana, ILINet 2017/18", ylab = ili_lab),
  list(src = "ilinet", loc = "30", season = "2019/20", title = "Montana, ILINet 2019/20", ylab = ili_lab),
  list(src = "ilinet", loc = "30", season = "2012/13", title = "Montana, ILINet 2012/13", ylab = ili_lab)))
```

A small state behaves the same way but with far more noise: Montana's ILINet values bounce between zero (plotted at $\varepsilon = 0.001$) and small positive numbers for weeks, so $M_t$ is set by isolated blips. In 2017/18 the series reached a plateau in week 23 and then just exceeded it in week 31, so $z$ sat at a small positive value (about 0.2) for eight weeks; in 2019/20 the same happened between weeks 26 and 32. These near-ties between an early high point and a slightly higher later one are hard for any model and are common in small states.

```{r fig-us}
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| fig-cap: "**United States**, ILINet 2017/18 and 2019/20 and FluSurv-NET 2017/18."
example_row(arr, rows, list(
  list(src = "ilinet", loc = "US", season = "2017/18", title = "US, ILINet 2017/18", ylab = ili_lab),
  list(src = "ilinet", loc = "US", season = "2019/20", title = "US, ILINet 2019/20", ylab = ili_lab),
  list(src = "flusurvnet", loc = "US", season = "2017/18", title = "US, FluSurv-NET 2017/18", ylab = "per 100k")))
```

National series are smooth and never near zero, so their early-season $z$ is lower (about 4–4.5 at week 10, versus 5–8 in the states) and declines steadily in small steps. ILINet 2019/20 again shows a first high point (week 22) narrowly exceeded later (week 28). ILINet and FluSurv-NET for the same 2017/18 national epidemic give similar $z$ curves, although FluSurv-NET peaked earlier (week 23 vs 27): a first hint that $z$ is comparable across sources.

# The distribution of the eventual z over the season

```{r fig-fan}
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "**Quantiles of the eventual $z$ by season week, for each source.** Bands are the 10–90% and 25–75% ranges across all training rows at that week; the line is the median. Same y-axis in all panels. FluSurv-NET begins at week 10 because its surveillance season starts in October."
zq <- ztab(rows, group, season_week)
ggplot(zq, aes(season_week, fill = group, color = group)) +
  pre_window() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q10, ymax = q90), alpha = 0.18, color = NA) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q25, ymax = q75), alpha = 0.38, color = NA) +
  geom_line(aes(y = q50), linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~group) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = SOURCE_COLORS, guide = "none") + scale_color_manual(values = SOURCE_COLORS, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_season_week(breaks = c(5, 10, 20, 30, 40)) +
  scale_y_continuous("eventual z (known only after the season)", limits = Z_LIM)
```

```{r fan-numbers}
pooled <- ztab(rows, season_week)
pw <- function(w, col = "q50") pooled[[col]][pooled$season_week == w]
zq_st <- zq |> filter(group == "ILINet states")
q_st <- function(w, col) zq_st[[col]][zq_st$season_week == w]
```

The three sources tell the same story: $z$ starts around 5–6.5 (median) before the window opens, declines roughly linearly through November and December, and collapses to 0 over January–February. Pooling all sources, the median eventual $z$ is `r f2(pw(10))` at week 10, `r f2(pw(15))` at week 15, `r f2(pw(20))` at week 20 and `r f2(pw(25))` at week 25 (@tbl-byweek). The spread is wide early (at week 10 the 25–75% range in ILINet states is `r f2(q_st(10, "q25"), 1)`–`r f2(q_st(10, "q75"), 1)`, i.e. peaks between `r round(exp(q_st(10, "q25")), -1)` and `r format(round(exp(q_st(10, "q75")), -2), big.mark = ",")` times the current record), and the upper end in October mostly reflects how close $M_t$ is to $\varepsilon$ (@sec-eps). For modelling, the early-season predictive distribution must be very wide on the log scale, and the spread shrinks sharply with $t$, so a constant-variance model for $z$ would be badly miscalibrated.

```{r tbl-byweek}
#| tbl-cap: "Median eventual $z$ [25%, 75%] and the share of rows with $z = 0$, by season week and source."
zq |> filter(season_week %in% c(5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40)) |>
  mutate(cell = paste0(f2(q50), " [", f2(q25), ", ", f2(q75), "]; ", percent(p0, 1))) |>
  select(week = season_week, group, cell) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = cell, values_fill = "–") |>
  kable()
```

## The atom at zero

```{r fig-atom}
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-cap: "**Share of training rows whose peak had already happened** (eventual $z = 0$ exactly), by season week and source."
ggplot(zq, aes(season_week, p0, color = group)) +
  pre_window() +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = SOURCE_COLORS) +
  scale_x_season_week() +
  scale_y_continuous("share of rows with z = 0\n(peak already reached)", labels = percent_format(1), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.02, 0.98), legend.justification = c(0, 1))
p0g <- function(g, w) zq$p0[zq$group == g & zq$season_week == w]
```

Before about week 17 (late November) almost no series has peaked; then the share with $z = 0$ climbs steeply, reaching `r pct(pw(20, "p0"))` at week 20, `r pct(pw(25, "p0"))` at week 25, `r pct(pw(30, "p0"))` at week 30 and `r pct(pw(35, "p0"))` at week 35 when all rows are pooled. By week 30 the share is `r pct(p0g("ILINet states", 30))` for ILINet states, `r pct(p0g("ILINet national + regions", 30))` for ILINet national/regions and `r pct(p0g("FluSurv-NET", 30))` for FluSurv-NET. The three curves are close, with FluSurv-NET slightly ahead in January (its hospitalization peaks tend to come a little earlier than ILINet's).

This atom is the central modelling fact: from January on, a large share of the outcome distribution is a point mass at 0, and a model must learn a probability of "already peaked" together with a continuous distribution for $z > 0$. Note that "already peaked" is itself not known in real time: a forecaster in week 25 does not know whether this week's record will be broken. A plain quantile regression can represent the atom (lower quantiles equal to 0); a Gaussian likelihood on $z$ or a model on $\log z$ cannot, which is why a two-part (hurdle) formulation or direct modelling of $k$ (weeks to peak) is natural.

# The eventual z by real-time stage features {#sec-stage}

The core features (the default feature set of `peak_gbqr`) describe where the season stands relative to its own record, and are all computable at week $t$:

- `wks_since_max`: how many weeks ago $M_t$ was set (0 = this week is a new record).
- `rel_max` $= \log(\text{current value}) - \log(M_t)$: how far below the record the current week is (0 = at the record; −0.7 ≈ half of it).
- `g1` $= \log(\text{this week}) - \log(\text{last week})$: one-week growth rate on the log scale (0.4 ≈ 50% increase).

```{r fig-stage}
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-cap: "**Eventual $z$ within bins of each real-time stage feature, at three season weeks** (all sources pooled). Thin line: 10–90% range; thick bar: 25–75%; black tick: median. Numbers above each bin: share of rows with eventual $z = 0$ and the number of rows. Same y-axis throughout."
st <- rows |> filter(season_week %in% c(16, 22, 28)) |>
  mutate(week_lab = paste0("Season week ", season_week, " (~", format(season_week_date("2017/18", season_week), "%b %d"), ")"),
         wsm_bin = factor(ifelse(wks_since_max >= 4, "4+", as.character(wks_since_max)), levels = c("0", "1", "2", "3", "4+")),
         rel_bin = cut(rel_max, c(-Inf, -1, -0.4, -0.1, -1e-9, 0.1),
                       labels = c("< −1", "−1 to −0.4", "−0.4 to −0.1", "−0.1 to 0", "at max (0)")),
         rel_bin = factor(rel_bin, levels = rev(levels(rel_bin))),
         g1_bin = cut(g1, c(-Inf, -0.15, 0.15, 0.4, Inf),
                      labels = c("falling\n< −0.15", "flat\n±0.15", "rising\n0.15–0.4", "fast\n> 0.4")))
quantile_bars(st, wsm_bin, "weeks since the max was set") /
  quantile_bars(st, rel_bin, "rel_max = log(current / M_t)") /
  quantile_bars(st, g1_bin, "g1 = log growth over the last week")
sb <- function(var, w, lvl) {
  x <- st |> filter(season_week == w, {{ var }} == lvl)
  list(p0 = mean(x$at_zero), med = median(x$z), n = nrow(x))
}
```

At week 16 (mid-November) almost nothing has peaked (0–7% at $z = 0$ in every bin), and the features mostly separate "still at baseline" from "starting to rise": series whose record was set 4+ weeks ago are ones where nothing has happened yet, and they have the *largest* eventual $z$ (median `r f2(sb(wsm_bin, 16, "4+")$med, 1)`, vs `r f2(sb(wsm_bin, 16, "0")$med, 1)` when the current week is a record). At week 22 (late December) the same feature partly flips meaning: a record set 4+ weeks ago now means the peak has passed in `r pct(sb(wsm_bin, 22, "4+")$p0)` of cases (vs `r pct(sb(wsm_bin, 22, "0")$p0)` when the current week is the record), but the median $z$ in that bin is still `r f2(sb(wsm_bin, 22, "4+")$med, 1)` because the other half are seasons that have not started. Growth is informative in the same period (`r pct(sb(g1_bin, 22, "falling\n< −0.15")$p0)` of falling series with g1 < −0.15 have peaked vs `r pct(sb(g1_bin, 22, "fast\n> 0.4")$p0)` of fast risers with g1 > 0.4), and by week 28 the features separate "peaked" from "not peaked" well (`r pct(sb(wsm_bin, 28, "4+")$p0)` at $z = 0$ in the "4+ weeks" bin and `r pct(sb(rel_bin, 28, "< −1")$p0)` in the "rel_max < −1" bin). But within the weeks that matter most, 17–26, the bins overlap heavily: **none of these three "shape" features strongly predicts the eventual $z$ on its own**. (One current feature does: `hist_rel`, the current record relative to the location's typical peak; see @sec-predictors.) This motivates the search for better real-time predictors in @sec-predictors. The direction of the relationships also changes with $t$, an argument for letting models interact stage features with season week (as tree models do automatically).

# The eventual z and the time to peak

The companion target is $k = \text{peak week} - t$, the number of weeks until the peak ($k \le 0$ means the peak has passed, which is exactly when $z = 0$). Like $z$, $k$ is only known in hindsight.

```{r fig-kz}
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "**Eventual $z$ against weeks-to-peak $k$, for rows that had not yet peaked** ($k \\ge 1$). Shading: number of rows (log scale). Black: median $z$ at each $k$ (where at least 20 rows). Same axes in all panels."
kz <- rows |> filter(k >= 1)
rho_kz <- kz |> group_by(group) |> summarise(rho = cor(k, z, method = "spearman"))
kmed <- kz |> group_by(group, k) |> summarise(med = median(z), n = n(), .groups = "drop") |> filter(n >= 20)
ggplot(kz, aes(k, z)) +
  geom_bin2d(bins = c(20, 18)) +
  geom_line(data = kmed, aes(k, med), color = INK, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_text(data = rho_kz, aes(x = 1, y = 9, label = paste0("Spearman ρ(k, z) = ", f2(rho))), hjust = 0, size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~group) +
  scale_x_log10("k = weeks until the peak (log scale)", breaks = c(1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32)) +
  scale_y_continuous("eventual z", limits = c(0, Z_LIM[2])) +
  scale_fill_distiller("rows", palette = "Blues", direction = 1, trans = "log10") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
kmed_all <- kz |> group_by(k) |> summarise(med = median(z))
km <- function(k) kmed_all$med[kmed_all$k == k]
k58 <- quantile(kz$z[kz$k >= 5 & kz$k <= 8], c(0.1, 0.9))
```

The relative size still to come grows steadily with the time until the peak: pooled across sources the median $z$ is `r f2(km(1))` one week before the peak, `r f2(km(2))` two weeks before, `r f2(km(4))` four weeks before, `r f2(km(8))` eight weeks before and `r f2(km(16))` sixteen weeks before; the Spearman correlation between $k$ and $z$ is `r f2(min(rho_kz$rho))`–`r f2(max(rho_kz$rho))` in every source. The spread at fixed $k$ is still large (for $k$ between 5 and 8 weeks, the 10–90% range of $z$ is `r f2(k58[1])`–`r f2(k58[2])`), but knowing $k$ removes much of the uncertainty in $z$. This supports modelling the two jointly, for example "size given timing": draw $k$ first, then $z$ given $k$ and the real-time features. The FluSurv-NET cluster at $z \approx 6$–8 with $k \approx 10$–20 is early-October rows with near-zero $M_t$ (the $\varepsilon$ effect again).

# Are the sources comparable?

```{r fig-compare}
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "**ILINet vs FluSurv-NET for the same locations and seasons.** Left: the 13 FluSurv-NET sites (all are states) paired with the same state's ILINet series; right: the US national series. Line: median eventual $z$; band: 25–75%; dotted: 90th percentile."
both <- inner_join(rows |> filter(source == "flusurvnet") |> distinct(location, season),
                   rows |> filter(source == "ilinet") |> distinct(location, season), by = c("location", "season"))
dm <- rows |> semi_join(both, by = c("location", "season")) |>
  mutate(panel = ifelse(location == "US", "United States", "FluSurv-NET sites (states) and the matching ILINet states"),
         src = ifelse(source == "ilinet", "ILINet", "FluSurv-NET"))
dq <- ztab(dm, panel, src, season_week)
ns <- dm |> distinct(panel, src, location, season) |> count(panel, src)
ggplot(dq, aes(season_week, color = src, fill = src)) +
  pre_window() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q25, ymax = q75), alpha = 0.25, color = NA) +
  geom_line(aes(y = q50), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_line(aes(y = q90), linetype = "dotted") +
  facet_wrap(~panel) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(ILINet = BLUE, `FluSurv-NET` = SOURCE_COLORS[["FluSurv-NET"]])) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(ILINet = BLUE, `FluSurv-NET` = SOURCE_COLORS[["FluSurv-NET"]])) +
  scale_x_season_week(breaks = c(5, 10, 20, 30, 40)) +
  scale_y_continuous("eventual z: median, 25–75% (band), 90% (dotted)", limits = Z_LIM)
wide <- dm |> filter(season_week >= WINDOW[1]) |> select(location, season, season_week, source, z) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = source, values_from = z) |> filter(!is.na(ilinet), !is.na(flusurvnet))
pk_pairs <- dm |> distinct(source, location, season, peak_week) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = source, values_from = peak_week)
mz <- function(src, w) median(dm$z[dm$location != "US" & dm$source == src & dm$season_week == w])
```

For the `r nrow(both)` (location, season) pairs that both sources cover (`r n_distinct(both$location)` locations, 2010/11–2022/23), the eventual $z$ distributions are very similar once the window opens: matched-state medians are `r f2(mz("ilinet", 15))` (ILINet) vs `r f2(mz("flusurvnet", 15))` (FluSurv-NET) at week 15, `r f2(mz("ilinet", 20))` vs `r f2(mz("flusurvnet", 20))` at week 20 and `r f2(mz("ilinet", 25))` vs `r f2(mz("flusurvnet", 25))` at week 25. Pair by pair, the Spearman correlation between the two sources' $z$ at the same location, season and week (weeks 10–43) is `r f2(cor(wide$ilinet, wide$flusurvnet, method = "spearman"))`, the median absolute difference is `r f2(median(abs(wide$ilinet - wide$flusurvnet)))`, and the median difference in peak week is `r median(pk_pairs$ilinet - pk_pairs$flusurvnet)`. The main disagreement is in October, when ILINet $z$ is higher because ILINet × percent positive is more often near zero at baseline. So pooling sources on the $z$ scale looks reasonable, provided the model has a source indicator for the baseline-level differences.

```{r fig-scale}
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "**Absolute vs relative scale.** Left: log of the season peak, one dot per series, in each source's own units. Right: eventual $z$ at season week 18 (early December), one dot per series. Black bar: 25–75% range, white tick: median."
peaks_r <- rows |> distinct(source, agg_level, location, season, .keep_all = TRUE)  # one row per series
z18 <- rows |> filter(season_week == 18)
strip <- function(df, col, xlab, title, show_y) {
  s <- df |> group_by(group) |> summarise(q25 = quantile({{ col }}, 0.25), q50 = median({{ col }}), q75 = quantile({{ col }}, 0.75))
  set.seed(1)
  ggplot(df, aes({{ col }}, group)) +
    geom_jitter(aes(color = group), height = 0.18, width = 0, size = 0.8, alpha = 0.4) +
    geom_linerange(data = s, aes(xmin = q25, xmax = q75, y = as.numeric(group) + 0.32), inherit.aes = FALSE,
                   linewidth = 2, color = INK) +
    geom_point(data = s, aes(q50, as.numeric(group) + 0.32), inherit.aes = FALSE, shape = "|", size = 4, color = "white") +
    scale_color_manual(values = SOURCE_COLORS, guide = "none") +
    scale_y_discrete(NULL, limits = rev, labels = if (show_y) waiver() else NULL) +
    labs(x = xlab, title = title) + theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
}
strip(peaks_r, log_peak, "log(peak + eps), in each source's own units", "Absolute peak size: not comparable across sources", TRUE) |
  strip(z18, z, "eventual z at season week 18", "Relative size z: on a common scale", FALSE)
lp <- peaks_r |> group_by(group) |> summarise(m = median(log_peak))
z18m <- z18 |> group_by(group) |> summarise(m = median(z))
```

On the absolute scale the sources live in different places: median log peaks of `r f2(lp$m[1])` (ILINet states; a peak of about `r f2(exp(lp$m[1]), 1)` in ILI × percent-positive units), `r f2(lp$m[2])` (ILINet national/regions) and `r f2(lp$m[3])` (FluSurv-NET, about `r round(exp(lp$m[3]))` per 100k). Pooling absolute peaks would need a source-specific location and scale at the very least. On the relative scale the distributions at week 18 overlap heavily (medians `r paste(f2(z18m$m), collapse = ", ")`).

# The role of eps {#sec-eps}

```{r fig-eps}
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "**Left:** share of rows where the running maximum is smaller than 10 × eps, i.e. essentially zero on the source's scale. **Right:** ILINet (all levels) median and 90th percentile of eventual $z$ recomputed with eps divided by 10, as used, and multiplied by 10."
near <- rows |> group_by(group, season_week) |> summarise(near = mean(M < 10 * eps), .groups = "drop")
ili <- rows |> filter(source == "ilinet") |> mutate(peak = exp(log_peak) - eps)
eps_q <- bind_rows(lapply(c(0.1, 1, 10), function(f) {
  ili |> mutate(zf = log(peak + eps * f) - log(M + eps * f)) |> group_by(season_week) |>
    summarise(median = median(zf), `90th percentile` = quantile(zf, 0.9)) |> mutate(factor = paste("eps ×", f))
})) |> pivot_longer(c(median, `90th percentile`), names_to = "stat")
p1 <- ggplot(near, aes(season_week, near, color = group)) +
  pre_window() + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = SOURCE_COLORS) +
  scale_x_season_week() + scale_y_continuous("share of rows with M_t < 10·eps", labels = percent_format(1)) +
  labs(title = "How often is the running max tiny?") +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.98, 0.98), legend.justification = c(1, 1))
p2 <- ggplot(eps_q, aes(season_week, value, color = stat, linetype = factor)) +
  pre_window() + geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(median = INK, `90th percentile` = "#9a9993")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(`eps × 0.1` = "dotted", `eps × 1` = "solid", `eps × 10` = "dashed")) +
  scale_x_season_week() + scale_y_continuous("eventual z (ILINet, all levels)", limits = c(0, 12)) +
  labs(title = "Sensitivity of ILINet z to eps") +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.98, 0.98), legend.justification = c(1, 1), legend.box = "horizontal")
p1 | p2
nr <- function(g, w) near$near[near$group == g & near$season_week == w]
eq <- function(f, st, w) eps_q$value[eps_q$factor == paste("eps ×", f) & eps_q$stat == st & eps_q$season_week == w]
```

Early in the season $M_t$ is frequently indistinguishable from zero: at week 10, $M_t < 10\varepsilon$ in `r pct(nr("ILINet states", 10))` of ILINet state rows, `r pct(nr("ILINet national + regions", 10))` of ILINet national/regional rows and `r pct(nr("FluSurv-NET", 10))` of FluSurv-NET rows; by week 15 this drops to `r pct(nr("ILINet states", 15))`, `r pct(nr("ILINet national + regions", 15))` and `r pct(nr("FluSurv-NET", 15))`; by week 20 it is essentially gone except for small ILINet states (`r pct(nr("ILINet states", 20))`). In these rows $z \approx \log(\text{peak}/\varepsilon)$, so its value is set by the choice of $\varepsilon$. The right panel shows how much: changing ILINet's $\varepsilon$ tenfold either way moves the median $z$ at week 5 from `r f2(eq(1, "median", 5))` to `r f2(eq(0.1, "median", 5))` or `r f2(eq(10, "median", 5))`, and the 90th percentile at week 10 from `r f2(eq(1, "90th percentile", 10))` to `r f2(eq(0.1, "90th percentile", 10))` or `r f2(eq(10, "90th percentile", 10))`; by week 15 the median barely moves (`r f2(eq(0.1, "median", 15))` / `r f2(eq(1, "median", 15))` / `r f2(eq(10, "median", 15))`) and by week 20 the curves coincide. Forecasts made in October–early November are therefore sensitive to $\varepsilon$ in the upper tail (on the peak scale this matters less, since $(M_t + \varepsilon)e^z$ largely undoes the change, but it does change what the model learns from pooled rows), and the relative $\varepsilon$ across sources determines how comparable their early-season rows are.

# Season-to-season variability

```{r fig-seasons}
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "**ILINet state-level series, one line per season.** Left: median eventual $z$ across states by week (dashed black: all seasons pooled). Right: share of states whose peak had passed. The earliest and latest seasons (by median state peak week) are highlighted."
sd_ <- rows |> filter(group == "ILINet states")
sz <- sd_ |> group_by(season, season_week) |> summarise(med = median(z), p0 = mean(at_zero), .groups = "drop")
spk <- sd_ |> distinct(location, season, peak_week) |> group_by(season) |> summarise(pk = median(peak_week))
early_s <- spk$season[which.min(spk$pk)]
late_s <- spk$season[which.max(spk$pk)]
sz <- sz |> mutate(hl = case_when(season == early_s ~ paste0(early_s, " (median peak wk ", min(spk$pk), ")"),
                                  season == late_s ~ paste0(late_s, " (median peak wk ", max(spk$pk), ")"),
                                  TRUE ~ "other seasons"))
pooled_st <- sd_ |> group_by(season_week) |> summarise(med = median(z))
hl_cols <- setNames(c(BLUE, ACCENT, "#b7b6b0"), c(unique(sz$hl[sz$season == early_s]), unique(sz$hl[sz$season == late_s]), "other seasons"))
p1 <- ggplot(sz, aes(season_week, med, group = season, color = hl, linewidth = hl != "other seasons")) +
  pre_window() + geom_line() +
  geom_line(data = pooled_st, aes(season_week, med), inherit.aes = FALSE, linetype = "dashed", color = INK) +
  scale_y_continuous("median eventual z across states", limits = Z_LIM) +
  labs(title = "Each line is one season (ILINet, states)")
p2 <- ggplot(sz, aes(season_week, p0, group = season, color = hl, linewidth = hl != "other seasons")) +
  pre_window() + geom_line() +
  scale_y_continuous("share of states already peaked", labels = percent_format(1)) +
  labs(title = "Timing differs by season, and z follows")
(p1 | p2) + plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
  scale_color_manual(values = hl_cols) & scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 1.2, `FALSE` = 0.4), guide = "none") &
  scale_x_season_week() & theme(legend.position = "top")
srange <- function(w) range(sz$med[sz$season_week == w])
```

Within a season, states move together: the "share already peaked" curves (right) rise steeply over a few weeks, and the season's position on the calendar varies a lot, from a median state peak in week `r min(spk$pk)` (`r early_s`) to week `r max(spk$pk)` (`r late_s`). Correspondingly, the median eventual $z$ across states at week 15 ranges from `r f2(srange(15)[1])` to `r f2(srange(15)[2])` across seasons, and at week 20 from `r f2(srange(20)[1])` to `r f2(srange(20)[2])`. This between-season variation is shared across locations and is the kind of variation a season-level random effect in a hierarchical model is meant to capture. It also means rows from the same season are strongly correlated, so the effective sample size for learning timing is closer to the number of seasons (`r cov_tab[["n seasons"]][1]` for ILINet states, `r cov_tab[["n seasons"]][2]` for ILINet national/regions) than to the number of rows, and validation must hold out whole seasons.

# Searching for better real-time predictors of z {#sec-predictors}

```{r load-predictors}
#| cache: false
pr <- read_rows("eda/predictor_rows.parquet")
fg <- readr::read_csv("eda/feature_groups.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
CURRENT <- fg$feature[fg$group == "current"]
grp_list <- function(sec) {
  x <- fg |> filter(section == sec)
  lapply(split(x$feature, factor(x$group, levels = unique(x$group))), identity)
}
G9 <- grp_list("section 9")
G11 <- grp_list("section 11")
HOL <- fg$feature[fg$group == "holiday"]
cv <- read_parquet("eda/cv_results.parquet")
cv_sets <- readr::read_csv("eda/cv_sets.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
boot <- readr::read_csv("eda/cv_bootstrap.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
imp <- readr::read_csv("eda/importance.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
pnums <- jsonlite::read_json("eda/predictors_numbers.json")
max_leak <- max(unlist(pnums$leakage_check_max_abs_change))
```

This is the part of the analysis that matters most for improving the models. We never see $z$ during a season, so the only way to predict it is through quantities we *can* compute at week $t$ that are associated with the eventual $z$. Below, **every candidate feature is real-time**: it uses only the current season's data through week $t$, and any "historical" quantity uses only **strictly earlier seasons** of the same source and location. The **eventual $z$ is the retrospective outcome** we check them against. We compute the candidates, look at their association with the eventual $z$ within narrow week bins (so that we are not just rediscovering "later in the season means smaller $z$"), and then ask the question that really matters: do they make cross-validated forecasts better? The features and the cross-validation are computed in Python (`relative_size_predictors.py`); this document summarizes their output.

## Candidate features

Notation used below, all known at week $t$: $\ell_s = \log(y_s + \varepsilon)$ is the log value in week $s$ (missing weeks are carried forward from the last observed week), $m = \log(M_t + \varepsilon)$ is the log running maximum, and "earlier seasons" means strictly earlier seasons of the same source and location. Most features are expressed **relative to $m$** (a difference of logs, i.e. a log ratio), for the same scale-free reason as $z$.

**Trend** (a/b). How the recent curve is moving.

- *Local polynomial ("Taylor") fits*, built the same way as the `TaylorFeature` used by the weekly GBQR models (`timeseriesutils.featurize.windowed_taylor_coefs` with trailing windows, whose design matrix has columns $1, u, u^2/2$), but on the log scale, without scaling, and with windows chosen for this problem: fit $\ell_s \approx b_0 + b_1 u + b_2 u^2/2$ by least squares to the last $W$ weeks, with $u = s - t = -W+1, \dots, 0$. `tay1_wW_*` are degree-1 fits (straight line; $W$ = 4, 6), `tay2_wW_*` degree-2 fits ($W$ = 6, 8). Features: `_lvl` $= b_0 - m$ (smoothed current level relative to the record; 0 = at the record), `_slope` $= b_1$ (smoothed weekly log growth; 0.2 ≈ +22% per week), `_curv` $= b_2$ (acceleration; negative = growth slowing, as it must before a peak). Missing if $t < W$.
- *Rolling means* `rm2`, `rm4` $= \log(\text{mean of the last 2 or 4 weeks} + \varepsilon) - m$ (`rm3` is already a model feature).
- *Lags* `lagL_rel` $= \ell_{t-L} - m$ for $L$ = 1–4: where the curve was $L$ weeks ago relative to today's record.

**Timing vs history** (c). Is it early or late relative to what is usual *here*?

- `t_minus_hist_pk` $= t - $ mean peak week of earlier seasons (negative = before the usual peak week); `t_minus_hist_pk_med` uses the median; `hist_pk_sd` is the standard deviation of earlier peak weeks (how predictable timing is at this location).
- `t_minus_clim_pk` $= t - $ mean peak week over *all* series (any source and location) of strictly earlier seasons.
- `hist_z_same_week`: the mean eventual $z$ at week $t$ in earlier seasons of this location (what "usually" remains at this point).

**Synchrony** (d). What are the *other* locations of the same source doing this season, as of week $t$? Computed over all non-national series of the same source and season observed at week $t$ (for ILINet, states and HHS regions together; the series itself is included).

- `sync_frac_past2`: share of locations whose record was set 2 or more weeks ago (0 before week 10).
- `sync_frac_half`: share whose current value is at least half their own record.
- `sync_med_rel_max`: median of `rel_max` across locations (0 = the typical location is at its record; negative = the typical location is already below its record).
- `sync_med_g3`: median 3-week log growth across locations (positive = the country is still rising).

**Onset** (e). Has the epidemic visibly started? Baseline $b$ = mean of $y$ over weeks 1 to min($t$, 8).

- `wks_since_onset2`, `wks_since_onset4`: weeks since the first week (from week 9 on) in which $y + \varepsilon \ge 2(b + \varepsilon)$ or $4(b + \varepsilon)$; −1 if not yet.
- `max_over_base` $= m - \log(b + \varepsilon)$ and `cur_over_base` $= \ell_t - \log(b + \varepsilon)$: how far above baseline the record and the current week are.

**Burden to date** (f). Cumulative incidence $C_t$ = sum of $y$ over weeks 5 to $t$ (the same sum as the model's `cum_rel`).

- `cum_vs_hist_total` $= \log(C_t + \varepsilon) - \log(\text{mean total over weeks 5–43 in earlier seasons} + \varepsilon)$: "how much of a typical season's burden has already happened" (0 = a full typical season's worth; −3 ≈ 5%).
- `cum_vs_hist_same_week` $= \log(C_t + \varepsilon) - \log(\text{mean } C_t \text{ at the same week in earlier seasons} + \varepsilon)$: ahead of (> 0) or behind (< 0) the typical cumulative curve.

**Level vs history** (g). `hist_rel` $= m - $ mean log peak of earlier seasons is already a model feature. New: `cur_vs_hist_peak` $= \ell_t - $ mean earlier log peak; `lvl_vs_hist_same_week` $= \ell_t - $ mean of $\ell$ at week $t$ in earlier seasons; `max_vs_hist_same_week` $= m - $ mean of $m$ at week $t$ in earlier seasons.

::: {.callout-note title="Checks against look-ahead"}
Every current-season feature at week $t$ is computed from a copy of the data with all weeks after $t$ deleted, and all history uses strictly earlier seasons. Perturbation tests confirm this (all give a maximum absolute change of exactly `r max_leak`): (1) replacing every value after week $t$ by 100× its value + 5 (for $t$ = 14, 22, 30) leaves all current-season features at week $t$ unchanged; (2) corrupting every series of 2015/16 and later seasons leaves the purely historical features of 2015/16 rows unchanged; (3) corrupting only the weeks after $t$ of the 2015/16 season leaves *every* feature of that season at week $t$ unchanged. The script also checks that its own recomputation of `rel_max` and `wks_since_max` matches `build_replay_rows` exactly (maximum difference `r pnums$consistency$max_abs_diff_rel_max`).
:::

## Which features move with the eventual z?

```{r fig-corr}
#| fig-height: 15
#| fig-cap: "**Within-week-bin Spearman correlation of each real-time feature with the eventual $z$ (left) and with the indicator that the peak is still ahead, $z > 0$ (right).** Rows are grouped: core features first, then each candidate group. Same colour scale in both panels; blue = higher feature value goes with smaller $z$."
ch <- corr_heatmap(pr, G9, setdiff(CURRENT, c("season_week", "src_code")), first_label = "core")
ch$plot
rz <- ch$data |> filter(target == "Spearman with z")
rng <- function(f, bins = c("wk 12–16", "wk 17–21", "wk 22–26"), d = rz) range(d$rho[d$feature == f & d$bin %in% bins])
timing_max <- max(abs(rz$rho[rz$feature %in% setdiff(G9[["timing vs history"]], "hist_z_same_week")]))
ser <- pr |> filter(!is.na(hist_rel)) |> distinct(source, agg_level, location, season, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  mutate(anom = log_peak - (lm - hist_rel))
anom_sd <- sd(ser$anom)
anom_q <- quantile(ser$anom, c(0.1, 0.9))
anom_sd_st <- sd(ser$anom[ser$group == "ILINet states"])
z_sd <- sd(pr$z[pr$season_week >= 17 & pr$season_week <= 26])
x1726 <- pr |> filter(season_week >= 17, season_week <= 26)
rho_hist_cum <- cor(x1726$hist_rel, x1726$cum_vs_hist_total, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs")
```

Three things stand out. First, the strongest associations by far belong to features that compare **this season's level with the same location's history**: `hist_rel` (in core) (`r f2(rng("hist_rel")[2])` to `r f2(rng("hist_rel")[1])` in weeks 12–26), and the burden feature `cum_vs_hist_total` (in SB) (`r f2(rng("cum_vs_hist_total")[2])` to `r f2(rng("cum_vs_hist_total")[1])`) and `max_vs_hist_same_week` (`r f2(rng("max_vs_hist_same_week")[2])` to `r f2(rng("max_vs_hist_same_week")[1])`). Read plainly: if the record so far is already as high as a typical peak here, little growth is left. This is partly built in, because $z = (\log \text{peak} - \text{typical log peak}) - \texttt{hist\_rel}$: the eventual $z$ splits exactly into a "size surprise" (how much bigger or smaller this season's peak is than this location's usual peak, which does not depend on $t$) and `hist_rel`, which we know. The size surprise has standard deviation `r f2(anom_sd)` (10–90% range `r f2(anom_q[1])` to `r f2(anom_q[2])`; `r f2(anom_sd_st)` for ILINet states), compared with a standard deviation of `r f2(z_sd)` for $z$ itself in weeks 17–26, so the history-relative level explains most of the variation in $z$ in the middle of the season, and what remains is the unpredictability of season size. Second, the shape-of-the-curve features (current `rel_max`, `g1`–`g3`, the new Taylor slopes and levels, lags) are weakly related to $z$ before week 22 (mostly $|\rho| < 0.4$) and become strong only in weeks 27–31, when they mainly tell us whether the peak has passed ($\rho \approx 0.5$–0.65 with $z > 0$). Third, **synchrony** features (`sync_med_rel_max`, `sync_med_g3`) track the national features closely and add a similar "is the country past its peak?" signal late in the season, while timing-vs-history features are nearly unrelated to $z$ within week bins ($|\rho| \le$ `r f2(timing_max)`, except `hist_z_same_week` at about `r f2(max(rng("hist_z_same_week", c("wk 12–16", "wk 17–21"))), 1)` before week 22), and onset features are weaker, noisier versions of the level features.

```{r fig-binned}
#| fig-height: 6.5
#| fig-cap: "**Eventual $z$ by decile of the most important features, at three week bins** (median and 25–75% band). `hist_rel` (in core) is shown first for comparison; the others are the top candidate features by LightGBM gain. Same y-axis as @fig-stage."
imp_main <- imp |> filter(`feature set` == "current + all new", model == "median quantile model") |> arrange(desc(gain_share))
top_new <- head(imp_main$feature[!imp_main$feature %in% CURRENT], 5)
binned_plot(pr, c("hist_rel", top_new), current = "hist_rel")
```

The binned plots show the shape of these relationships. `hist_rel` and `cum_vs_hist_total` give nearly straight, parallel lines: each unit increase in the log record relative to history (or in log cumulative burden relative to a typical season) removes about one unit of remaining growth, with little dependence on the week. The two are close substitutes (Spearman `r f2(rho_hist_cum)` with each other in weeks 17–26). The synchrony and trend features show much flatter relationships with wide bands, useful mainly for separating "peaked" from "not yet" in weeks 22–26.

## Do they improve forecasts? Leave-one-season-out cross-validation

```{r cv-main}
order9 <- cv_sets$set[order(cv_sets$order)]
rel9 <- cv_rel(cv, "current")
rp <- function(s, b = "all", rel = rel9) rel$rel_pinball[rel$set == s & rel$bin == b]
dl <- function(s, b = "all", rel = rel9) rel$d_logloss[rel$set == s & rel$bin == b]
gain <- function(s, b = "all", rel = rel9) 1 - rp(s, b, rel)
sb_main <- function(s, what = "seasons_better", metric = "pinball") boot_get(boot, "main", s, "current", metric, what)
n_cv_rows <- nrow(cv |> filter(set == "current"))
n_seasons_cv <- n_distinct(cv$season)
n_all_new <- length(unlist(G9))
```

Association is not the same as predictive value, particularly when a candidate feature largely duplicates one already in core. The real test is whether adding a feature improves **out-of-sample** forecasts of the eventual $z$ for a season the model has not seen.

**Design.** We hold out one whole season at a time (all sources and locations of that season; `r n_seasons_cv` folds, 1997/98–2022/23), fit on all other seasons, and forecast the held-out season's rows. Holding out whole seasons matters because rows from the same season are strongly correlated (@fig-seasons). Models: LightGBM quantile regression of $z$ at levels 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 0.9 (200 trees, learning rate 0.05, 15 leaves, at least 50 rows per leaf), scored by **pinball loss** averaged over the five levels (the standard proper score for quantile forecasts; lower is better), and a LightGBM classifier for $z > 0$ with the same settings, scored by **log loss** (lower is better). To keep runtime modest, CV uses the even season weeks only (`r format(n_cv_rows, big.mark = ",")` of `r format(nrow(pr), big.mark = ",")` rows). Feature sets: (i) core, the `r length(CURRENT)` default features; (ii–vii) core + one candidate group; (viii) core + all `r n_all_new` candidate features; single-group ablations from (viii); and two combinations suggested by the results. All $`r length(order9)` \times `r n_seasons_cv` \times 6 = `r format(length(order9) * n_seasons_cv * 6, big.mark = ",")`$ fits took about 5 minutes (4 single-threaded processes).

```{r fig-cv}
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| fig-cap: "**Cross-validated skill of each feature set relative to core.** Left: mean pinball loss for $z$, as a ratio to core (below 1 = better). Right: change in log loss for $z > 0$ (below 0 = better). Circles: week bins; diamond: all weeks. The ablation \"core − hist_rel\" is off the scale (see table)."
cv_dotplot(rel9, setdiff(order9, "current − hist_rel"), "core")
```

```{r tbl-cv-pinball}
#| tbl-cap: "Mean pinball loss of the eventual $z$ relative to core, by week bin (leave-one-season-out; values below 1 are improvements)."
kable(cv_table(rel9, rel_pinball, order9))
abs_cur <- rel9 |> filter(set == "current")
```

Absolute pinball loss of core: `r paste(f2(abs_cur$pinball[abs_cur$bin != "all"], 3), collapse = ", ")` in the six bins, `r f2(abs_cur$pinball[abs_cur$bin == "all"], 3)` overall.

```{r tbl-cv-logloss}
#| tbl-cap: "Change in log loss for $z > 0$ relative to core (negative values are improvements)."
kable(cv_table(rel9, d_logloss, order9))
```

Log loss of core: `r f2(abs_cur$logloss[abs_cur$bin == "17–21"], 3)` in weeks 17–21, `r f2(abs_cur$logloss[abs_cur$bin == "22–26"], 3)` in 22–26, `r f2(abs_cur$logloss[abs_cur$bin == "27–31"], 3)` in 27–31, `r f2(abs_cur$logloss[abs_cur$bin == "all"], 3)` overall.

```{r cv-main-numbers}
S <- "+ synchrony"; B <- "+ burden to date"; SBs <- "+ synchrony + burden"; SBL <- "+ synchrony + burden + level"
TR <- "+ trend (Taylor, rolling means, lags)"; ON <- "+ onset"; TI <- "+ timing vs history"; AN <- "+ all new"
bins_sb <- sapply(c("5–11", "12–16", "17–21", "22–26"), function(b) pct(gain(SBs, b), 0.1))
sync_bins <- sapply(c("5–11", "12–16", "17–21"), function(b) gain(S, b))
imp_top <- imp_main |> head(2)
```

What the cross-validation shows:

- **`hist_rel` is the single most valuable core feature.** Dropping it makes the quantile forecasts `r pct(rp("current − hist_rel") - 1)` worse overall (about `r f2(mean(c(rp("current − hist_rel", "17–21"), rp("current − hist_rel", "22–26"))), 1)` times the loss in weeks 17–26) and raises the log loss by `r f2(dl("current − hist_rel"), 3)`. core already has the strongest predictor we found.
- **Synchrony and burden-to-date are the only groups that help consistently, and they help together.** Adding the four synchrony features reduces pinball loss by `r pct(gain(S), 0.1)` overall (by `r pct(min(sync_bins), 0.1)`–`r pct(max(sync_bins), 0.1)` in each bin from week 5 to 21) and beats core in `r sb_main(S)` of `r n_seasons_cv` held-out seasons. Adding the two burden features reduces it by `r pct(gain(B), 0.1)` overall and by `r pct(gain(B, "22–26"), 0.1)` in weeks 22–26. **Adding both reduces pinball loss by `r pct(gain(SBs), 0.1)` overall: `r paste(bins_sb, collapse = ", ")` in weeks 5–11, 12–16, 17–21 and 22–26, with `r ifelse(abs(gain(SBs, "27–31")) < 0.005, "no change", pct(gain(SBs, "27–31"), 0.1))` in 27–31 and a `r pct(-gain(SBs, "32–43"), 0.1)` loss in 32–43** (where $z$ is almost always 0 and absolute losses are tiny). It beats core in `r sb_main(SBs)` of `r n_seasons_cv` seasons, and in `r pct(sb_main(SBs, "boot_win"), 0.1)` of season-level bootstrap resamples (weeks 12–31). Adding the level-vs-history group as well gives about the same result (`r pct(gain(SBL), 0.1)` better, `r sb_main(SBL)` of `r n_seasons_cv` seasons).
- **Taylor/trend, onset and timing-vs-history features do not help.** Trend features lower pinball loss by a negligible `r pct(gain(TR), 0.1)` overall (they are worse in weeks 17–21 and better only in weeks 32–43) and beat core in only `r sb_main(TR)` of `r n_seasons_cv` seasons; onset features have no effect (`r pct(-gain(ON), 0.1)`); timing-vs-history features make forecasts `r pct(-gain(TI), 0.1)` worse (`r pct(-gain(TI, "12–16"), 1)` worse in weeks 12–16). The trend information is already carried by `rel_max`, `g1`–`g3` and `rm3`, and timing-vs-history has too few past seasons per location (0–10 for ILINet states) to be reliable.
- **Adding everything is worse than adding the right few.** All `r n_all_new` candidate features together make forecasts `r pct(-gain(AN), 0.1)` worse overall, even though they help in weeks 22–26 (`r pct(-gain(AN, "22–26"), 0.1)`); removing the timing group from that set recovers a `r pct(gain("all − timing vs history"), 0.1)` gain. With only `r n_seasons_cv` seasons, extra noisy features give the trees more ways to overfit season-specific patterns.
- **No candidate improves the probability that the peak is still ahead.** Every feature set other than the `hist_rel` ablation changes the $z > 0$ log loss by between `r f2(min(rel9$d_logloss[rel9$bin == "all" & rel9$set != "current − hist_rel"]), 3)` and +`r f2(max(rel9$d_logloss[rel9$bin == "all" & rel9$set != "current − hist_rel"]), 3)` overall, with no consistent gains in any week bin. Whether the peak has passed is already captured by the national and local stage features (the gain importances of the full model are dominated by `` `r imp_top$feature[1]` ``, `r pct(imp_top$gain_share[1])` of total gain, and `` `r imp_top$feature[2]` ``, `r pct(imp_top$gain_share[2])`; @fig-importance).

```{r fig-importance}
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-cap: "**LightGBM gain importance** for the median ($\\tau = 0.5$) quantile model with all core and candidate features, fitted to all CV rows. Grey: core features; blue: candidate features."
imp_main |> head(25) |>
  mutate(feature = factor(feature, levels = rev(feature)), kind = ifelse(feature %in% CURRENT, "current", "new")) |>
  ggplot(aes(gain_share, feature, fill = kind)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(current = "#b7b6b0", new = BLUE), labels = c(current = "core features", new = "candidate features")) +
  scale_x_continuous("share of total gain", labels = percent_format(1)) + labs(y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), legend.position = c(0.98, 0.05), legend.justification = c(1, 0))
```

## Recommendation

```{r idm-check}
idm <- unlist(pnums$consistency$idmodels_feature_max_abs_diff)
```

1. **Synchrony and burden-to-date: adopted as feature set SB.** The four synchrony features and the two burden-to-date features (`sync_med_rel_max`, `sync_med_g3`, `sync_frac_past2`, `sync_frac_half`, `cum_vs_hist_total`, `cum_vs_hist_same_week`) are available in idmodels 8c56bf0 as `sync_burden_features = True`. Evidence: `r pct(gain(SBs), 0.1)` lower cross-validated pinball loss overall and `r pct(gain(SBs, "22–26"), 0.1)` lower in weeks 22–26 (late December to late January, when size forecasts matter most), better in `r sb_main(SBs)` of `r n_seasons_cv` held-out seasons. (In `idmodels.peak.series` the burden features agree with the ones used here to within `r formatC(max(idm[grepl("cum", names(idm))]), format = "e", digits = 0)`; its synchrony features differ slightly, by up to `r f2(max(idm[grepl("sync", names(idm))]))`, because it uses the carried-forward definition, whereas this document uses reported-at-t. In the model pipeline, `peak_gbqr__sb` gave slightly better peak-size and slightly worse timing forecasts than `peak_gbqr` on the ILINet development seasons, so core remains the default.)
2. **Keep `hist_rel`**, which is the most important single predictor; any change to how the historical log peak is computed (e.g. how many earlier seasons, what to do when there are none, as for `r pct(mean(is.na(pr$hist_rel)), 0.1)` of rows) should be treated as a change to the model's main input.
3. **Do not add the Taylor/trend, onset or timing-vs-history features** for now; they add no skill and in some week bins hurt. Do not expect any of these features to improve the "already peaked?" probability.
4. **Caveats.** The gains are modest and were measured with one fixed LightGBM configuration on ILINet and FluSurv-NET only (NHSN excluded); they should be confirmed in the actual `peak_gbqr` pipeline and on the NHSN test seasons. Synchrony features need all locations of a source to be reported at week $t$, which holds for NHSN in real time, but with real-time (unrevised) data they will be noisier than here, where we used final data throughout. In leave-one-season-out, training seasons later than the held-out season carry "history" that includes the held-out season; this does not leak the held-out season's outcomes into its own features, but it means history-based features were fit with slightly more history than a real-time model would have.

# Holiday weeks {#sec-holiday}

## Why holidays might matter

ILINet's main ingredient is **% ILI**: the share of all outpatient visits that are for influenza-like illness. Around Christmas and New Year many routine visits (check-ups, elective appointments) are postponed while sick people still come in, so the *denominator* shrinks and % ILI can jump even if the number of flu cases does not. If that happens, a running maximum set during the holidays may be partly artificial: an "initial peak" that the real epidemic later exceeds. FluSurv-NET counts laboratory-confirmed hospitalizations per 100,000 people; it has no visit denominator, so it is a useful contrast. (Hospitalizations can still genuinely rise over the holidays, e.g. because of holiday gatherings, so a bump in both sources would point to a real epidemic effect rather than an artefact.)

```{r holiday-cal}
cal <- readr::read_csv("eda/holiday_calendar.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

We call a week a **holiday week** if its Saturday week-ending date falls between **December 22 and January 7**. That is two or three weeks per season: season weeks `r min(cal$season_week)`–`r max(cal$season_week)`, i.e. MMWR weeks 51, 52 and 53 or 1 (@tbl-holcal). The calendar is known in advance, so any feature based on it is real-time.

```{r tbl-holcal}
#| tbl-cap: "Holiday weeks (week-ending Saturday in Dec 22 – Jan 7) in each training season."
cal |> group_by(season) |>
  summarise(`season weeks` = paste(season_week, collapse = ", "),
            `week-ending dates` = paste(format(as.Date(date), "%b %d"), collapse = ", "),
            `MMWR weeks` = paste(mmwr_week, collapse = ", ")) |>
  kable()
```

## Is there a holiday spike, and is it specific to ILINet?

For each series we compare the log value in each holiday week with the average log value of the two weeks before and the two weeks after the holiday block (the **holiday excess**; 0.4 means about 50% above the surrounding weeks). The same calculation for blocks shifted 6 weeks earlier or later is a placebo: it shows how big the "excess" is simply from the curvature of the epidemic curve.

```{r fig-holexcess}
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "**Left:** mean holiday excess by source, with placebo blocks 6 weeks earlier and later (95% intervals from resampling seasons). **Right:** ILINet minus FluSurv-NET excess for the same location and season, by position within the holiday block."
ex <- read_parquet("eda/holiday_excess.parquet") |> mutate(group = factor(group, levels = SOURCE_GROUPS))
blocks <- c("placebo −6 wk", "holiday", "placebo +6 wk")
exs <- ex |> group_by(group, block) |>
  summarise(ci = list(cluster_ci(excess, season)), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(mean = sapply(ci, `[`, "mean"), lo = sapply(ci, `[`, "lo"), hi = sapply(ci, `[`, "hi"),
         block = factor(block, levels = blocks))
hx <- ex |> filter(block == "holiday")
pair <- inner_join(hx |> filter(source == "ilinet"), hx |> filter(source == "flusurvnet"),
                   by = c("location", "season"), suffix = c("_ili", "_fsn"))
pdiff <- bind_rows(lapply(0:2, function(k) {
  dk <- pair[[paste0("excess_k", k, "_ili")]] - pair[[paste0("excess_k", k, "_fsn")]]
  ok <- !is.na(dk)
  if (sum(ok) < 10) return(NULL)
  ci <- cluster_ci(dk[ok], pair$season[ok])
  tibble(pos = c("1st holiday\nweek", "2nd", "3rd")[k + 1], mean = ci["mean"], lo = ci["lo"], hi = ci["hi"], n = sum(ok))
}), {
  ci <- cluster_ci(pair$excess_ili - pair$excess_fsn, pair$season)
  tibble(pos = "block\nmean", mean = ci["mean"], lo = ci["lo"], hi = ci["hi"], n = nrow(pair))
}) |> mutate(pos = factor(pos, levels = pos))
p1 <- ggplot(exs, aes(block, mean, color = group)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = INK2) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = SOURCE_COLORS) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("6 weeks earlier\n(placebo)", "holiday weeks\n(Dec 22 – Jan 7)", "6 weeks later\n(placebo)")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "mean log excess vs 2 weeks before + 2 after", title = "Holiday excess by source") +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.02, 0.98), legend.justification = c(0, 1))
p2 <- ggplot(pdiff, aes(pos, mean)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = INK2) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), shape = 18, size = 0.6) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "ILINet excess − FluSurv-NET excess", title = paste0("Same location & season (", nrow(pair), " pairs)"))
(p1 | p2) + plot_layout(widths = c(1.3, 1))
ciq <- function(g, b = "holiday") exs |> filter(group == g, block == b)
cis <- function(r, d = 2) paste0(f2(r$mean, d), " (", f2(r$lo, d), "–", f2(r$hi, d), ")")
placebo_rng <- range(exs$mean[exs$block != "holiday"])
# how often the peak falls in a holiday week vs the 3 weeks either side
hw <- cal |> group_by(season) |> summarise(first = min(season_week), last = max(season_week), nh = n())
pk_h <- rows |> distinct(source, agg_level, location, season, .keep_all = TRUE) |> left_join(hw, by = "season") |>
  mutate(in_hol = peak_week >= first & peak_week <= last,
         near = (peak_week >= first - 3 & peak_week < first) | (peak_week > last & peak_week <= last + 3)) |>
  group_by(group) |> summarise(per_week_hol = mean(in_hol) / mean(nh), per_week_near = mean(near) / 6)
pkh <- function(g, col) pk_h[[col]][pk_h$group == g]
pdk <- function(p) pdiff |> filter(pos == p)
```

There is a clear holiday bump, **but it is just as large in FluSurv-NET as in ILINet**: mean excess `r cis(ciq("ILINet states"))` for ILINet states, `r cis(ciq("ILINet national + regions"))` for ILINet national/regions and `r cis(ciq("FluSurv-NET"))` for FluSurv-NET, against placebo values between `r f2(placebo_rng[1])` and `r f2(placebo_rng[2])`. Epidemic peaks also fall in holiday weeks more often than in nearby weeks, and about equally in both sources: per week, `r pct(pkh("ILINet states", "per_week_hol"), 0.1)` of ILINet state peaks and `r pct(pkh("FluSurv-NET", "per_week_hol"), 0.1)` of FluSurv-NET peaks fall in a holiday week, versus `r pct(pkh("ILINet states", "per_week_near"), 0.1)` and `r pct(pkh("FluSurv-NET", "per_week_near"), 0.1)` per week in the three weeks either side. So most of the holiday bump is a real feature of the epidemics, seen in hospitalizations too. What does differ is the **timing within the block** (right panel). For the same location and season, ILINet's excess is `r f2(pdk("1st holiday\nweek")$mean)` higher (`r f2(pdk("1st holiday\nweek")$lo)`–`r f2(pdk("1st holiday\nweek")$hi)`) in the first holiday week and `r f2(-pdk("3rd")$mean)` lower (`r f2(pdk("3rd")$lo)` to `r f2(pdk("3rd")$hi)`) in the third week (early January), with no clear difference in the block average (`r f2(pdk("block\nmean")$mean)`, `r f2(pdk("block\nmean")$lo)` to `r f2(pdk("block\nmean")$hi)`). That is the pattern the denominator story predicts: ILINet runs ahead of hospitalizations over Christmas and then drops back at New Year. (Part of it may also be that outpatient ILI generally leads hospitalizations by about a week.)

## Are holiday-week maxima less likely to be the real peak?

```{r fig-holmax}
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "**Share of running maxima that turned out to be the final peak, by how many weeks ago the maximum was set,** for rows at season weeks 20–30, split by whether the maximum was set in a holiday week. Eventual $z = 0$ means the maximum was the final peak."
hm <- pr |> filter(season_week >= 20, season_week <= 30, wks_since_max >= 1, wks_since_max <= 5) |>
  mutate(where = ifelse(max_in_holiday == 1, "max set in a holiday week", "max set in another week")) |>
  group_by(group, where, wks_since_max) |> summarise(p0 = mean(at_zero), n = n(), .groups = "drop")
ggplot(hm, aes(wks_since_max, p0, color = group, linetype = where)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(~group) +
  scale_color_manual(values = SOURCE_COLORS, guide = "none") +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("max set in a holiday week" = "solid", "max set in another week" = "dashed")) +
  scale_y_continuous("share whose max was the final peak\n(eventual z = 0)", labels = percent_format(1), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "weeks since the running max was set")
hmv <- function(g, w, hol) pct(hm$p0[hm$group == g & hm$wks_since_max == w &
                                     hm$where == ifelse(hol, "max set in a holiday week", "max set in another week")])
hmp <- function(g) paste(sapply(1:3, function(w) paste(hmv(g, w, TRUE), "vs", hmv(g, w, FALSE))), collapse = ", ")
```

This is where ILINet and FluSurv-NET part ways. Compare maxima set the same number of weeks ago, in the same part of the season. In **ILINet**, maxima set in a holiday week are **less** often the final peak than maxima set in other weeks, at least in the first three weeks after they are set. For ILINet states it is `r hmp("ILINet states")` one, two and three weeks after the max was set. For ILINet national and regional series it is `r hmp("ILINet national + regions")`. In **FluSurv-NET** there is no such penalty: `r hmp("FluSurv-NET")`. (Some of the gap is timing: other-week maxima in this window tend to be set later in the season, when a peak is more likely. That confound affects FluSurv-NET equally, and FluSurv-NET shows no gap.) So an ILINet holiday maximum is more often an "initial peak" that is later exceeded, which supports the idea that holiday maxima in ILINet deserve discounting.

```{r holpost}
post <- pr |> filter(weeks_since_holiday_end >= 1, weeks_since_holiday_end <= 4) |>
  group_by(source = group, `weeks after holidays` = weeks_since_holiday_end) |>
  summarise(rows = n(), share_hol = mean(max_in_holiday == 1),
            p0_hol = mean(at_zero[max_in_holiday == 1]), p0_oth = mean(at_zero[max_in_holiday == 0]),
            med_hol = median(z[max_in_holiday == 1]), med_oth = median(z[max_in_holiday == 0]),
            q90_hol = quantile(z[max_in_holiday == 1], 0.9), q90_oth = quantile(z[max_in_holiday == 0], 0.9),
            .groups = "drop")
pp <- function(g, w, col) post[[col]][post$source == g & post$`weeks after holidays` == w]
```

@tbl-holpost looks at the weeks right after the holidays. One week after the holiday block, `r pct(pp("ILINet states", 1, "share_hol"))` of ILINet state series have their running maximum in a holiday week (`r pct(pp("FluSurv-NET", 1, "share_hol"))` for FluSurv-NET). Those maxima are *already* more often final than the other maxima in the same week (`r pct(pp("ILINet states", 1, "p0_hol"))` vs `r pct(pp("ILINet states", 1, "p0_oth"))` for ILINet states), because they are older, not because they are more reliable.

```{r tbl-holpost}
#| tbl-cap: "Rows 1–4 weeks after the last holiday week: share whose running maximum was set in a holiday week, and the eventual $z$ given where the maximum was set."
post |> mutate(across(c(share_hol, p0_hol, p0_oth), ~ percent(.x, 1)), across(c(med_hol, med_oth, q90_hol, q90_oth), f2)) |>
  rename(`max in holiday week` = share_hol, `P(z=0) holiday max` = p0_hol, `P(z=0) other max` = p0_oth,
         `median z holiday max` = med_hol, `median z other max` = med_oth, `q90 z holiday max` = q90_hol,
         `q90 z other max` = q90_oth) |>
  kable()
```

## Real-time holiday features

All use only data through week $t$ and the calendar:

- `hol_now` = 1 if week $t$ is a holiday week.
- `max_in_holiday` = 1 if the running maximum $M_t$ was set in a holiday week (only from week 10).
- `weeks_since_holiday_end` = −1 before the holiday block, 0 during it, and $t - (\text{last holiday week})$ afterwards, capped at 10.
- A **holiday-adjusted running maximum** $M^{nh}_t$: the largest in-window value in weeks 10 to $t$ **excluding holiday weeks** (before week 10, the latest value, as for $M_t$). From it:
  - `holiday_excess_max` $= \log(M_t + \varepsilon) - \log(M^{nh}_t + \varepsilon)$: 0 unless the running maximum is a holiday week. When it is, this is how far that holiday value sits above the best non-holiday week.
  - `rel_max_nohol` $= \ell_t - \log(M^{nh}_t + \varepsilon)$ and `wks_since_max_nohol` $= t - (\text{week of } M^{nh}_t)$: `rel_max` and `wks_since_max` recomputed against the adjusted maximum.

The perturbation checks described earlier (@sec-predictors) also cover these features, with no change.

## Do holiday features improve forecasts?

Same leave-one-season-out design as above (`r n_seasons_cv` folds, even weeks). Results are reported for all rows and separately for ILINet and FluSurv-NET rows, for all weeks, weeks 17–31, the holiday weeks themselves, and 1–3 and 4–6 weeks after the holidays (the weeks where a holiday maximum could mislead).

```{r holiday-cv}
cvh <- read_parquet("eda/cv_holiday.parquet")
meta <- pr |> select(source, agg_level, location, season, season_week, weeks_since_holiday_end, hol_now)
hbin <- function(w, h) case_when(w >= 1 & w <= 3 ~ "1–3 wk after", w >= 4 & w <= 6 ~ "4–6 wk after",
                                 h == 1 ~ "holiday weeks", TRUE ~ "other weeks")
hol_sets <- c("+ holiday", "+ holiday flags", "+ holiday-adjusted max", "+ synchrony + burden", "+ synchrony + burden + holiday")
hol_bins <- c("all weeks", "weeks 17–31", "holiday weeks", "1–3 wk after", "4–6 wk after")
xh <- cvh |> left_join(meta, by = c("source", "agg_level", "location", "season", "season_week")) |>
  mutate(hb = hbin(weeks_since_holiday_end, hol_now), src = ifelse(source == "ilinet", "ILINet", "FluSurv-NET"))
hol_summary <- function(x) {
  bind_rows(
    x |> group_by(set) |> summarise(p = mean(pinball), l = mean(logloss)) |> mutate(weeks = "all weeks"),
    x |> filter(season_week >= 17, season_week <= 31) |> group_by(set) |> summarise(p = mean(pinball), l = mean(logloss)) |>
      mutate(weeks = "weeks 17–31"),
    x |> filter(hb != "other weeks") |> group_by(set, weeks = hb) |> summarise(p = mean(pinball), l = mean(logloss), .groups = "drop")
  ) |> group_by(weeks) |> mutate(ratio = p / p[set == "current"], dll = l - l[set == "current"]) |> ungroup()
}
hs <- bind_rows(hol_summary(xh) |> mutate(rows = "all"),
                hol_summary(xh |> filter(src == "ILINet")) |> mutate(rows = "ILINet"),
                hol_summary(xh |> filter(src == "FluSurv-NET")) |> mutate(rows = "FluSurv-NET")) |>
  filter(set != "current")
hv <- function(r, s, w, col = "ratio") hs[[col]][hs$rows == r & hs$set == s & hs$weeks == w]
hol_tab <- function(col, d) hs |> select(rows, `feature set` = set, weeks, v = all_of(col)) |>
  mutate(weeks = factor(weeks, levels = hol_bins), rows = factor(rows, levels = c("all", "ILINet", "FluSurv-NET")),
         `feature set` = factor(`feature set`, levels = hol_sets)) |>
  arrange(rows, `feature set`, weeks) |> mutate(v = formatC(v, format = "f", digits = d)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = weeks, values_from = v)
hb_get <- function(s, ref, metric, what) boot_get(boot, "holiday", s, ref, metric, what)
```

```{r fig-holcv}
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-cap: "**Cross-validated pinball loss of the eventual $z$ relative to core, by source of the rows and weeks relative to the holidays.** Same x-axis in both panels."
hs |> filter(rows != "all", weeks %in% c("all weeks", "holiday weeks", "1–3 wk after", "4–6 wk after")) |>
  mutate(set = factor(vlabel(set), levels = vlabel(rev(hol_sets))), weeks = factor(weeks, levels = c("all weeks", "holiday weeks", "1–3 wk after", "4–6 wk after")),
         rows = factor(paste(rows, "rows"), levels = c("ILINet rows", "FluSurv-NET rows"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(ratio, set, color = weeks, shape = weeks == "all weeks")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, color = INK2) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.6), size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~rows) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`all weeks` = INK, `holiday weeks` = "#9ecae1", `1–3 wk after` = "#4292c6", `4–6 wk after` = "#08306b")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 18, `FALSE` = 16), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "pinball loss relative to core", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

```{r tbl-holcv}
#| tbl-cap: "Pinball loss relative to core (below 1 = better)."
kable(hol_tab("ratio", 3))
```

```{r tbl-holcvll}
#| tbl-cap: "Change in log loss for $z > 0$ relative to core (below 0 = better)."
kable(hol_tab("dll", 4))
```

The holiday features **do not improve the quantile forecasts of $z$**. Adding all six changes pinball loss by `r sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * (hv("all", "+ holiday", "all weeks") - 1))` overall and by `r sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * (hv("all", "+ holiday", "1–3 wk after") - 1))` in the 1–3 weeks after the holidays, for all rows, and by `r sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * (hv("ILINet", "+ holiday", "all weeks") - 1))` and `r sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * (hv("ILINet", "+ holiday", "1–3 wk after") - 1))` for ILINet rows alone. The adjusted-maximum trio does slightly better, but only on FluSurv-NET rows (`r sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * (hv("FluSurv-NET", "+ holiday-adjusted max", "all weeks") - 1))` overall, `r sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * (hv("FluSurv-NET", "+ holiday-adjusted max", "1–3 wk after") - 1))` 1–3 weeks after, from few rows). Added on top of synchrony + burden, the holiday features make things worse (`r f2(hv("all", "+ synchrony + burden + holiday", "all weeks"), 3)` vs `r f2(hv("all", "+ synchrony + burden", "all weeks"), 3)` relative to current overall; synchrony + burden alone is better in `r pct(1 - hb_get("+ synchrony + burden + holiday", "+ synchrony + burden", "pinball", "boot_win"))` of season bootstrap resamples). For the probability that the peak is still ahead, the holiday features help very slightly: log loss `r f2(hv("all", "+ holiday", "all weeks", "dll"), 4)` overall and `r f2(hv("all", "+ holiday", "1–3 wk after", "dll"), 3)` in the 1–3 weeks after the holidays (`r f2(hv("FluSurv-NET", "+ holiday", "all weeks", "dll"), 3)` overall for FluSurv-NET rows, `r f2(hv("ILINet", "+ holiday", "all weeks", "dll"), 3)` for ILINet rows). That is small against a log loss of about 0.28 at those weeks and is not consistent across seasons (better in `r hb_get("+ holiday", "current", "logloss", "seasons_better")` of `r n_seasons_cv` seasons). Added to synchrony + burden, they remove most of that set's small log-loss penalty (Δ = `r f2(hv("all", "+ synchrony + burden + holiday", "all weeks", "dll"), 4)` vs +`r f2(hv("all", "+ synchrony + burden", "all weeks", "dll"), 4)`; better in `r hb_get("+ synchrony + burden + holiday", "+ synchrony + burden", "logloss", "seasons_better")` of `r n_seasons_cv` seasons) but cost pinball loss.

## Would adjusting the ILINet training data be better?

```{r holiday-adjust}
shift <- unlist(pnums$holiday$adjust_shift)
cva <- read_parquet("eda/cv_holiday_adjust.parquet") |>
  left_join(meta, by = c("source", "agg_level", "location", "season", "season_week")) |>
  mutate(hb = hbin(weeks_since_holiday_end, hol_now))
ref_a <- cva |> filter(data == "ILINet as reported", set == "current")
adj <- bind_rows(
  cva |> group_by(data, set) |> summarise(p = mean(pinball), l = mean(logloss), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(weeks = "all weeks", ratio = p / mean(ref_a$pinball), dll = l - mean(ref_a$logloss)),
  cva |> filter(hb != "other weeks") |> group_by(data, set, weeks = hb) |> summarise(p = mean(pinball), .groups = "drop") |>
    left_join(ref_a |> filter(hb != "other weeks") |> group_by(weeks = hb) |> summarise(pr = mean(pinball)), by = "weeks") |>
    mutate(ratio = p / pr)
)
av <- function(d, s, w = "all weeks") adj$ratio[adj$data == d & adj$set == s & adj$weeks == w]
n_fsn_folds <- n_distinct(cva$season)
```

An alternative to a feature is to fix the ILINet series before computing targets and features.
